items.prompt: A machine learning engineer wants every production model version to be traceable to the training code, data, and parameters that produced it, so that any prediction can be audited and the model can be reproduced. Which practice best supports this MLOps goal?

choices.text: Train in notebooks and record the data and parameters in a shared document after each run.
Log training with MLflow Tracking, including parameters, metrics, and the model, and register the model in Unity Catalog so its version links back to the run.
Save the model file to a cloud storage folder named with the date of training.
Overwrite one registered model version each time a new model is trained so that only the latest is kept.

items.explanation: MLflow Tracking records parameters, metrics, artifacts, and code context for each run. A model registered in Unity Catalog keeps a link to its source run, and Unity Catalog adds lineage and governance. Together they give reproducibility and auditability.

choiceRationales.A: Manual documentation is error-prone and is not linked to the model artifact, so it does not give reliable traceability.
choiceRationales.C: Date-named folders store files but do not capture parameters, metrics, data, or code, and offer no governance or versioning.
choiceRationales.D: Registered model versions are immutable and new training creates a new version. Keeping only the latest would destroy the history needed for audit and rollback.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.1: Identify the best practices of an MLOps strategy.

items.prompt: A team follows MLOps best practices on Databricks with separate dev, staging, and prod environments and Unity Catalog. Which two practices align with the recommended approach? Choose two.

choices.text: Separate environments by using different catalogs, such as dev, staging, and prod, and control access with Unity Catalog permissions.
Let data scientists manually edit models in the prod catalog so that fixes reach production quickly.
Use model aliases such as champion and challenger, and have inference code load models:/prod.ml.fraud@champion.
Use the workspace model registry stages Staging and Production to mark which version is live.

items.explanation: Databricks recommends isolating environments, for example with separate catalogs governed by Unity Catalog permissions. Aliases such as champion let inference code reference a stable name while the alias is reassigned to a new validated version. Stages belong to the legacy workspace registry, and manual edits in prod bypass review and validation.

choiceRationales.B: Manual changes in prod skip testing, review, and automation. Production assets should be changed through automated, reviewed deployment.
choiceRationales.D: Stages are a feature of the legacy workspace model registry and are deprecated. Unity Catalog uses aliases and tags instead.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.1: Identify the best practices of an MLOps strategy.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer creates a cluster to train a PyTorch model on GPUs. The engineer wants the cluster to start with GPU drivers and common deep learning frameworks already installed and configured to work together. Which cluster configuration should the engineer choose?

choices.text: A standard Databricks Runtime on a GPU instance type, then install CUDA and the frameworks with init scripts
Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning with a GPU-enabled version on a GPU instance type
Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning on a CPU-only instance type
A SQL warehouse with a GPU-enabled size

items.explanation: Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning includes GPU-enabled versions that come with GPU libraries and popular deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow preinstalled and tested together. Pairing a GPU ML runtime with a GPU instance type avoids manual driver and library setup.

choiceRationales.A: This can be made to work, but it is the manual setup and version matching that the ML runtime is designed to remove.
choiceRationales.C: The ML runtime is right, but a CPU-only instance has no GPUs to accelerate training.
choiceRationales.D: SQL warehouses run SQL analytics workloads and are not used to train PyTorch models.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.2: Identify the advantages of using ML runtimes.

items.prompt: A data scientist moves an existing scikit-learn and MLflow training notebook from a standard Databricks Runtime cluster to a Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning cluster. Which two advantages should the data scientist expect? Choose two.

choices.text: Popular ML libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost, and MLflow are preinstalled with compatible versions.
Models trained on the cluster are automatically registered in Unity Catalog and deployed to a serving endpoint.
Built-in support for distributed training and hyperparameter tuning tools, such as Hyperopt and Horovod, is included.
Training no longer needs a cluster because the runtime executes on serverless compute only.

items.explanation: Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning is built on the standard runtime and adds preinstalled, compatible ML libraries along with tools for distributed training and hyperparameter tuning. It does not register or deploy models on its own, and it still runs on compute.

choiceRationales.B: Registration and serving are explicit steps, such as logging with MLflow and creating a Model Serving endpoint. The runtime does not do them automatically.
choiceRationales.D: The ML runtime is a runtime version selected for a cluster or compute resource. It does not remove the need for compute.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.2: Identify the advantages of using ML runtimes.

items.prompt: A data scientist runs a Databricks AutoML regression experiment on a table with many columns, including a numeric column with a single constant value and an ID column. The data scientist wants to understand how AutoML handled these columns and which algorithms it tried. Where can this information be found?

choices.text: In the generated data exploration notebook and the trial notebooks, which show the data profile and the code for each algorithm and its hyperparameters
Only in the best trial's registered model in Unity Catalog, because AutoML does not keep the other trials
In the Feature Engineering client, which stores AutoML's selected features as a feature table
In the Mosaic AI Model Serving endpoint logs, which record the algorithms evaluated during training

items.explanation: AutoML generates a data exploration notebook that profiles the dataset, and a editable notebook for each trial showing the algorithm, preprocessing, and hyperparameters. Each trial is logged to MLflow, so the data scientist can compare all trials and not just the best one.

choiceRationales.B: AutoML logs every trial as an MLflow run with its own notebook. Nothing is automatically registered, and non-best trials are kept.
choiceRationales.C: AutoML does not write its feature selection into a feature table. Feature handling is visible in the trial notebooks.
choiceRationales.D: Serving endpoints serve models after deployment. They do not record training-time algorithm search.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.3: Identify how AutoML facilitates model/feature selection.

items.prompt: A data scientist uses Databricks AutoML to train a classification model and wants to understand how AutoML supports model selection. Which two statements are correct? Choose two.

choices.text: AutoML trains multiple candidate models using different algorithms and hyperparameters, and ranks the trials by a chosen evaluation metric.
AutoML automatically promotes the best model to the champion alias in Unity Catalog without user action.
AutoML trial results are logged to MLflow, so the user can compare trials and identify the best model.
AutoML guarantees that the best model needs no further validation, because it searches all possible algorithms.

items.explanation: AutoML runs many trials with different algorithms and hyperparameters and ranks them by a metric. Trials are tracked in MLflow, so they can be compared and the best one selected. Promotion and validation remain the user's responsibility.

choiceRationales.B: AutoML does not assign aliases or register the model automatically. The user registers and promotes it.
choiceRationales.D: AutoML searches a limited set of algorithms and does not remove the need for validation.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.3: Identify how AutoML facilitates model/feature selection.

items.prompt: A data scientist is new to a regression problem on a tabular Delta table. They want a strong baseline quickly and need to show stakeholders how it was built. Which advantage of Databricks AutoML best fits this need?

choices.text: It guarantees the best possible model, so no further tuning or review is needed.
It generates editable notebooks with the source code for each trial, so the baseline can be inspected and customized.
It replaces the need to log runs to MLflow because results are stored in a separate proprietary format.
It automatically deploys the best model to a Model Serving endpoint without any configuration.

items.explanation: Databricks AutoML follows a glass-box approach. It trains and tunes several models and generates a notebook with the source code for each trial, plus a data exploration notebook. This lets a data scientist inspect, reproduce, and modify the baseline. AutoML does not guarantee an optimal model, and it does not deploy models automatically.

choiceRationales.A: AutoML gives a good baseline, but it does not guarantee the best model. Domain knowledge and further iteration are still valuable.
choiceRationales.C: AutoML logs its trials to MLflow experiments. It does not use a separate proprietary format.
choiceRationales.D: AutoML does not deploy models on its own. You register and serve the model as a separate step.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.4: Identify the advantages AutoML brings to the model development process.

items.prompt: A team lead wants to adopt Databricks AutoML for a binary classification project. Which TWO advantages does AutoML bring to the model development process? (Choose two.)

choices.text: It automatically performs data preparation steps such as imputing missing values and encoding categorical features as part of its trials.
It removes the need for a labeled target column in the training data.
It trains and compares multiple algorithms with hyperparameter tuning, with each trial tracked as an MLflow run.
It automatically promotes the best model to the champion alias in Unity Catalog.

items.explanation: AutoML applies basic preprocessing such as imputation and categorical encoding. It also trains and tunes several algorithms and logs every trial as an MLflow run, so results are easy to compare. It still needs a labeled target for supervised problems. It does not set registry aliases for you.

choiceRationales.B: Classification and regression are supervised, so AutoML needs a target column that you specify.
choiceRationales.D: AutoML does not assign registry aliases such as champion. You choose and register a model, then set the alias yourself.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.4: Identify the advantages AutoML brings to the model development process.

items.prompt: An ML engineer created a feature table in the legacy workspace Feature Store in workspace A. A data scientist in workspace B, which is attached to the same Unity Catalog metastore, needs those features for training. Which benefit of creating the feature table in Unity Catalog instead addresses this need?

choices.text: The table is copied automatically into every workspace in the account, so each workspace keeps its own local replica.
The data scientist must be added to the workspace A access control list before the table can be read.
The table is governed at the metastore level, so a user in any attached workspace can read it once granted privileges in Unity Catalog.
The table must first be published to an online store before other workspaces can read it.

items.explanation: A feature table in Unity Catalog is a Delta table with a primary key that lives in the metastore, not in one workspace. Any workspace attached to that metastore can use it, and access is controlled with Unity Catalog privileges such as SELECT. A workspace feature table is scoped to the workspace that created it.

choiceRationales.A: Unity Catalog does not replicate tables into each workspace. The same governed table is accessed from every attached workspace.
choiceRationales.B: Per-workspace ACLs describe the legacy workspace Feature Store limitation. Unity Catalog uses metastore-level privileges instead.
choiceRationales.D: An online store is for low-latency serving. It is not required for cross-workspace offline reads for training.

items.prompt: A team is deciding whether to migrate its workspace feature tables to Unity Catalog. Which two statements describe benefits of Unity Catalog feature tables? Choose two.

choices.text: Feature tables are governed with the same Unity Catalog privileges and three-level namespace as other data assets.
Feature tables no longer need a primary key, because Unity Catalog generates row identifiers automatically.
Feature tables are automatically published to an online store, so real-time serving needs no extra setup.
Lineage links feature tables to the models and notebooks that use them, and the tables can be discovered in Catalog Explorer.

items.explanation: Unity Catalog feature tables are governed like other UC data. They use catalog.schema.table names and GRANT-based access, and lineage and discovery come with them. A primary key is still required, and online serving needs separate publishing.

choiceRationales.B: A Unity Catalog feature table must still have a primary key constraint. Unity Catalog does not generate one.
choiceRationales.C: Offline feature tables are not published to an online store automatically. You set up online serving separately.

items.prompt: A data engineer has a Spark DataFrame `features_df` with one row per customer and a `customer_id` column. They want to create a feature table named `main.ml.customer_features` in Unity Catalog so that rows can be updated by key later. Which call should they use?

choices.text: FeatureStoreClient().create_table(name='main.ml.customer_features', primary_keys=['customer_id'], df=features_df)
FeatureEngineeringClient().create_table(name='main.ml.customer_features', primary_keys=['customer_id'], df=features_df)
FeatureEngineeringClient().create_table(name='main.ml.customer_features', df=features_df)
mlflow.register_model(features_df, 'main.ml.customer_features')

items.explanation: In Unity Catalog, feature tables are created with FeatureEngineeringClient.create_table using a three-level name. A primary key is required, so the table can be merged into by key later. The DataFrame can supply the schema and initial data.

choiceRationales.A: FeatureStoreClient is the older workspace feature store client from databricks-feature-store. It is not the current practice for Unity Catalog feature tables.
choiceRationales.C: This omits primary_keys, which a Unity Catalog feature table requires.
choiceRationales.D: The MLflow model registry registers models, not feature tables. It does not take a DataFrame.

items.prompt: A data scientist is creating a Unity Catalog feature table from daily customer snapshots and wants to support point-in-time lookups when building training sets. Which two actions should they take? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Include the timestamp column in the table's primary key and pass it to create_table with timeseries_columns
Use the timestamp column as the only primary key and leave customer_id as a regular column
Use FeatureLookup with timestamp_lookup_key set to the column in the training DataFrame that holds the event time
Set the Delta table property delta.enableChangeDataFeed on the training DataFrame instead of the feature table

items.explanation: A point-in-time feature table has a timestamp key column in its primary key, which is declared as a time series column. When building the training set, a FeatureLookup with timestamp_lookup_key tells Databricks which event time to use. It then returns the latest feature values at or before that time for each entity.

choiceRationales.B: The entity key such as customer_id must remain in the primary key. A timestamp alone does not identify the entity.
choiceRationales.D: Change data feed is unrelated to point-in-time lookups, and it is a table property, not something set on a DataFrame.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer maintains a Unity Catalog feature table with FeatureEngineeringClient. A streaming job computes new feature values and must write them to the table. Which two statements about FeatureEngineeringClient.write_table are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Passing mode="overwrite" replaces the entire contents of a Unity Catalog feature table.
The df argument can be a streaming DataFrame, so the feature table is updated continuously.
Passing mode="append" adds rows and allows duplicate primary key values.
The DataFrame being written must include the table's primary key columns.

items.explanation: write_table merges the DataFrame into the existing feature table. It matches rows on the primary key, so the key columns must be present. It accepts streaming DataFrames, which lets a streaming job keep the table current.

choiceRationales.A: Unity Catalog feature tables are written with merge semantics. Rows are upserted by primary key, and the table is not replaced wholesale.
choiceRationales.C: Append is not the supported write mode, and a feature table must keep one row per primary key, so duplicate keys are not allowed.

resources.title: Work with feature tables in Unity Catalog

items.prompt: A data scientist has a Spark DataFrame, features_df, with a unique customer_id column and several computed features. They want to create the Unity Catalog feature table main.ml.customer_features and populate it with this data in one step. Which call should they use?

choices.text: fe.write_table(name="main.ml.customer_features", df=features_df, mode="merge")
FeatureStoreClient().create_feature_table("customer_features", keys="customer_id", features_df=features_df)
fe.create_table(name="main.ml.customer_features", primary_keys=["customer_id"], df=features_df)
features_df.write.format("delta").saveAsTable("main.ml.customer_features")

items.explanation: With FeatureEngineeringClient, create_table takes the three-level table name, the primary keys, and an optional DataFrame. The DataFrame defines the schema and supplies the initial rows. After that, write_table updates the table.

choiceRationales.A: write_table updates a feature table that already exists. It does not create one, so this call fails if the table is missing.
choiceRationales.B: This is the older workspace Feature Store client API, which is deprecated. It is not the current way to create Unity Catalog feature tables.
choiceRationales.D: This creates a plain Delta table with no primary key constraint, so it is not a valid feature table. A primary key must be defined.

items.prompt: A data scientist has a DataFrame of customer IDs and churn labels. They want to train a model using features stored in a Unity Catalog feature table, joined by customer_id. Which approach should they use?

choices.text: Join the DataFrame to the feature table manually with Spark, then call mlflow.sklearn.log_model on the model.
Define FeatureLookup objects for the feature table, then call FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set with the DataFrame, the lookups, and the label column.
Call FeatureEngineeringClient.write_table on the labels DataFrame to merge the labels into the feature table.
Create a FeatureLookup for each row of the DataFrame and pass them to mlflow.register_model.

items.explanation: FeatureLookup objects specify which features to fetch from a feature table and which key to join on. FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set joins them to the labeled DataFrame, and load_df() then returns the training data. Logging the model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model and the training set also records the feature lineage.

choiceRationales.A: A manual join can produce a working model, but it does not record feature metadata. The model could not automatically look up features at inference time.
choiceRationales.C: write_table creates or updates feature table data. It does not build a training set, and labels do not belong in the feature table.
choiceRationales.D: Lookups are defined per feature table and key, not per row. mlflow.register_model registers a model and does not assemble training data.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.8: Train a model with features from a feature store table.

items.prompt: An ML engineer has created a training set with FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set. They plan to train a scikit-learn model and log it so features are looked up automatically at inference. Choose two actions that are correct.

choices.text: Call training_set.load_df() and convert the result to pandas to get the training data, including the label column.
Call training_set.load_df() and drop the label column, because the feature store supplies labels at training time.
Log the model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model, passing the training_set argument.
Log the model with mlflow.sklearn.log_model, which automatically records the feature table lookups.

items.explanation: load_df() returns a DataFrame with the original columns, including the label, plus the looked-up features, so it is the source of training data. FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model with the training_set packages the model with feature lookup metadata. This lets batch scoring or serving fetch features by key.

choiceRationales.B: Labels come from the DataFrame you supplied, not from the feature store. Dropping the label would leave nothing to train against.
choiceRationales.D: Plain mlflow.sklearn.log_model does not record feature lookup metadata. Use FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model with the training set instead.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.8: Train a model with features from a feature store table.

items.prompt: A data scientist logged a model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model, passing a training set built from FeatureLookup objects. The model is registered in Unity Catalog. A batch job has a Spark DataFrame containing only the lookup key column (customer_id). Which call should the job use to produce predictions with features automatically retrieved from the feature table?

choices.text: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(model_uri).predict(df)
fe.score_batch(model_uri=model_uri, df=df)
fe.read_table(name=feature_table).join(df, "customer_id").predict()
fe.create_training_set(df, feature_lookups, label=None).predict(model_uri)

items.explanation: When a model is logged with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model, it stores feature lookup metadata. FeatureEngineeringClient.score_batch uses that metadata to look up features by key from the feature tables, joins them to the input DataFrame, and applies the model. The input only needs the lookup keys (plus any non-feature inputs).

choiceRationales.A: Loading the model as a plain pyfunc and predicting on a DataFrame with only customer_id would fail, because the feature columns are not supplied and no lookup is done.
choiceRationales.C: Manually reading and joining the table is possible, but the DataFrame has no predict method, and it bypasses the automatic lookup the logged model provides.
choiceRationales.D: create_training_set builds datasets for training, and a TrainingSet object has no predict method. It is not the scoring API.

items.prompt: A team logged a model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model and registered it in Unity Catalog. They want it to retrieve features automatically at inference time. Which TWO statements are true? (Choose two.)

choices.text: The input to score_batch must include every feature column so the model can run.
The input DataFrame must include the lookup key columns used to join to the feature tables.
The model must be re-trained each time the feature table values are updated, or scoring will fail.
The caller needs permission to read the feature tables, since they are retrieved during scoring.

items.explanation: A model logged with feature lookup metadata needs the lookup keys in the input so it can join feature values. Features are read from the Unity Catalog feature tables at scoring time, so the caller needs access to those tables. Features need not be supplied, and updated feature values do not require retraining just to score.

choiceRationales.A: Incorrect. The point of the packaged lookup metadata is that features are retrieved automatically, so only the keys (and any non-feature inputs) are required.
choiceRationales.C: Incorrect. Scoring reads the current feature values; retraining is a modeling decision and is not required for scoring to work.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer maintains a Unity Catalog feature table that is used for nightly batch training. The team now needs a real-time Mosaic AI Model Serving endpoint to retrieve the same features with low latency. Which statement correctly describes the difference between the offline feature table and an online feature table?

choices.text: The offline table is a Delta table in Unity Catalog suited to large-scale batch reads for training and batch inference. The online table is a copy of that data in a low-latency store for serving real-time lookups.
The offline table stores only the latest value per primary key, and the online table stores the full history of feature values for point-in-time training.
The offline table is used only for storing model artifacts, and the online table is used only for storing feature definitions.
The offline and online tables are unrelated datasets, so features must be computed separately and by different code for each.

items.explanation: The offline feature table is a Delta table in Unity Catalog, which is optimized for large batch scans used in training and batch scoring. An online table or online store holds a copy of the feature data in a low-latency store so serving endpoints can look up features by primary key in milliseconds. The online copy is kept in sync from the offline table, so the feature logic is defined once.

choiceRationales.B: This reverses the roles. Online stores typically serve the latest value per key, while the offline Delta table can hold more data and supports point-in-time lookups for training.
choiceRationales.C: Neither table type stores model artifacts or feature definitions. Both hold feature values.
choiceRationales.D: The online table is derived from the offline table. Publishing it avoids duplicated logic and training-serving skew.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.10: Describe the differences between online and offline feature tables.

items.prompt: A data scientist is reviewing the design of a feature store used for both model training and real-time inference. Which TWO statements correctly describe online versus offline feature tables? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Offline feature tables are Delta tables that are well suited to batch workloads such as building training sets and running batch inference.
Online feature tables are best for scanning billions of historical rows to build large training datasets.
Online feature tables support low-latency lookups by primary key, which suits real-time serving.
Offline feature tables must be used to answer individual lookups within milliseconds at inference time.

items.explanation: Offline feature tables are Delta tables in Unity Catalog, which are built for high-throughput batch reads such as training set creation and batch scoring. Online feature tables are built for fast primary-key lookups, so a serving endpoint can retrieve features at request time. Each fits a different access pattern.

choiceRationales.B: Large historical scans are an offline workload. Online stores are optimized for single-key lookups, not bulk scans.
choiceRationales.D: Millisecond per-key lookups are the job of the online store. Offline Delta tables are not designed for that latency.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.10: Describe the differences between online and offline feature tables.

items.prompt: A data scientist trained many models in one MLflow experiment and logged an `auc` metric for each (higher is better). Some runs failed or are still running. Using `MlflowClient`, which call returns the single best completed run?

choices.text: client.search_runs([experiment_id], filter_string="attributes.status = 'FINISHED'", order_by=["metrics.auc"], max_results=1)[0]
client.search_runs([experiment_id], filter_string="attributes.status = 'FINISHED'", order_by=["metrics.auc DESC"], max_results=1)[0]
client.get_run(experiment_id).data.metrics["auc"]
client.search_runs([experiment_id], max_results=1)[0], because results are sorted by best metric by default

items.explanation: `MlflowClient.search_runs` accepts a `filter_string` to keep only finished runs and an `order_by` list to sort on a metric. Since a higher AUC is better, you sort descending and keep one result. Without an explicit order, results are not sorted by metric quality.

choiceRationales.A: Without DESC, the sort is ascending, so this returns the run with the lowest AUC, which is the worst run.
choiceRationales.C: `get_run` takes a run ID, not an experiment ID. It fetches one known run and does not search or compare runs.
choiceRationales.D: The default ordering is by start time, newest first, not by metric. This also does not exclude failed or running runs.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.11: Identify the best run using the MLflow Client API.

items.prompt: An ML engineer uses `MlflowClient.search_runs` to find the run with the lowest `val_loss` in an experiment, so that its model can be registered afterward. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Passing order_by=["metrics.val_loss ASC"] and max_results=1 returns the run with the lowest logged val_loss.
Runs are returned sorted by best metric value by default, so the first result is always the best run.
run.data.metrics["val_loss"] holds the full per-epoch history of the metric for that run.
The returned run's run.info.run_id can be used to build a runs:/<run_id>/model URI for registering the model.

items.explanation: Ordering by `metrics.val_loss ASC` with `max_results=1` gives the lowest value. The best run's `run_id` then forms the `runs:/<run_id>/model` URI used to register the model. `search_runs` does not rank by metric unless you ask it to, and `run.data.metrics` holds only the latest value of each metric.

choiceRationales.B: The default order is by start time, newest first. You must set `order_by` to rank by a metric.
choiceRationales.C: `run.data.metrics` holds only the latest value for each metric. The full history is available through `client.get_metric_history`.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.11: Identify the best run using the MLflow Client API.

items.prompt: A data scientist trains a model in a custom loop inside an active MLflow run. They plan to log results by calling MLflow tracking APIs manually. Which two statements about manual logging are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: mlflow.log_metric can store a text value such as "xgboost" as a metric, so the algorithm name can be filtered in the UI.
mlflow.log_metrics accepts a dictionary of metric names and numeric values, so several metrics can be logged in one call.
mlflow.log_param can be called again with a new value for the same key in the same run to overwrite the earlier value.
mlflow.log_artifacts uploads all files in a local directory to the run's artifact location.

items.explanation: Metrics must be numeric, and mlflow.log_metrics lets you log a dictionary of them in one call. mlflow.log_artifacts uploads the contents of a local directory to the run's artifact location, which suits a folder of plots or reports. Parameters are immutable within a run, and text values belong in params or tags.

choiceRationales.A: Metrics must be numeric. Text such as an algorithm name belongs in a parameter or a tag.
choiceRationales.C: Parameters are write-once per key in a run. Logging a different value for an existing key raises an error instead of overwriting it.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 1.12: Manually log metrics, artifacts, and models in an MLflow Run.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer trains a scikit-learn model and logs it manually in an MLflow run. They want the logged model to record the expected input and output schema, so that callers get schema validation at inference time. What should they do?

choices.text: Log the list of feature column names with mlflow.log_param and read it back when serving.
Save the model with pickle and upload the file with mlflow.log_artifact.
Create a signature with mlflow.models.infer_signature and pass it to mlflow.sklearn.log_model.
Call mlflow.log_dict on the training DataFrame's schema after the model is logged.

items.explanation: A model signature describes the input and output schema and is stored in the MLmodel file when you pass it to the flavor's log_model function. infer_signature builds it from sample inputs and predictions. MLflow can then enforce the schema when the model is loaded as a pyfunc model or served.

choiceRationales.A: A parameter is only a string on the run. It is not a model signature and MLflow does not use it to validate inputs.

items.prompt: A data scientist has computed `mean` and `std` for the `sensor_value` column of a Spark DataFrame. Rows with a null `sensor_value` must be kept so they can be imputed later, and rows more than 3 standard deviations from the mean must be removed. Which filter does this?

choices.text: df.filter(abs(col("sensor_value") - mean) <= 3 * std)
df.filter(abs(col("sensor_value") - mean) > 3 * std)
df.filter(col("sensor_value").isNull() | (abs(col("sensor_value") - mean) <= 3 * std))
df.na.drop(subset=["sensor_value"]).filter(abs(col("sensor_value") - mean) <= 3 * std)

items.explanation: In Spark SQL, comparing a null value returns null, and `filter` treats null as false, so a plain range condition silently drops null rows. Adding an explicit `isNull()` check with OR keeps the nulls while still removing values beyond 3 standard deviations.

choiceRationales.A: This removes the outliers but also drops null rows, because the comparison evaluates to null and the row is filtered out.
choiceRationales.B: This keeps only the outliers, which is the opposite of the goal. It also drops nulls.
choiceRationales.D: `na.drop` removes the null rows explicitly, so they cannot be imputed later.

choiceRationales.C: Mode is mainly suited to categorical data. For a continuous column, exact repeats may be rare, and no single-value imputation preserves variance.

Nulls are treated as missing along with the configured `missingValue`. Imputer works only on numeric columns.

choiceRationales.B: Imputer is an Estimator. You must call fit() to compute the surrogate values. The resulting ImputerModel is the Transformer.
choiceRationales.D: Imputer supports only numeric input columns, even with the mode strategy. Categorical string columns need another approach, such as filling with the most frequent value computed manually or via fillna.

items.prompt: A data scientist trains a Spark ML model on a numeric column that has missing values. They want the same training-derived median to be used to fill missing values whenever the model scores new data. What should they do?

choices.text: Call `Imputer.fit()` on each incoming scoring DataFrame before calling `transform()`.
Apply `df.fillna(0)` to the scoring DataFrame before prediction.
Add an `Imputer` with `strategy="median"` as a stage in the `Pipeline`, fit the pipeline on the training data, and log the resulting `PipelineModel` with MLflow.
Compute the median of the scoring DataFrame with `approxQuantile` and fill the missing values with it.

items.explanation: Fitting the pipeline on training data stores the training median in the fitted `ImputerModel`. Logging the `PipelineModel` with MLflow packages that value with the model, so scoring applies the same imputation. This keeps training and inference consistent and avoids leaking information from scoring data.

choiceRationales.A: Refitting on scoring data computes a new median from that batch, so it differs from the training median and varies between batches.
choiceRationales.B: Filling with 0 ignores the training median and can distort the feature distribution.
choiceRationales.D: This also uses a median from the scoring data rather than the training data, which causes training-serving inconsistency.

items.prompt: A data scientist indexes a string column `color` that has four distinct values with `StringIndexer`. They then apply `OneHotEncoder` with its default settings to the indexed column. What does the encoded output look like for a row whose category received the highest index (3)?

choices.text: A length-4 vector with a 1 in the last position
A length-3 vector with a 1 in the last position
A length-3 vector of all zeros
A null value, because the highest index is dropped from the data

items.explanation: Spark's `OneHotEncoder` has `dropLast=True` by default, so four categories produce a vector of length 3. The category with index 3 is the dropped one and is represented by all zeros. This avoids perfectly collinear features in linear models. Setting `dropLast=False` gives a length-4 vector.

choiceRationales.A: This would need `dropLast=False`. With the default, the vector has one fewer element than the number of categories.
choiceRationales.B: A length of 3 is right, but index 3 is the dropped category, so it has no 1 in any position.
choiceRationales.D: The row is kept and the encoder does not produce null. The dropped category is represented by an all-zero vector.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer is building a Spark ML pipeline and plans to use `OneHotEncoder` on a categorical feature. Which two statements about `OneHotEncoder` are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Its input column must be numeric category indices, such as the output of `StringIndexer`.
It accepts a raw string column directly and indexes it internally.
It adds one separate DataFrame column for each category.
It outputs a single vector column, which is stored as a sparse vector.

items.explanation: In Spark ML, `OneHotEncoder` takes numeric category indices, so a string column must first go through `StringIndexer`. It writes a single vector column, typically a `SparseVector`, rather than separate columns per category. That vector column can go straight into `VectorAssembler`.

choiceRationales.B: `OneHotEncoder` does not index strings. Use `StringIndexer` first.
choiceRationales.C: The result is one vector-typed column that holds all the category positions. It does not add a column per category.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer is preparing a dataset with a high-cardinality categorical column, merchant_id, which has about 200,000 distinct values. They plan to train a gradient-boosted tree model. Which statement best describes one-hot encoding for this column?

choices.text: It is required, because tree-based models cannot split on numeric columns derived from categories.
It is a poor fit, because it would create about 200,000 sparse columns, so a more compact representation such as target encoding, hashing, or learned embeddings is usually better.
It is ideal, because it adds no extra columns and preserves the category ordering.
It is appropriate only if the values are first scaled with StandardScaler.

items.explanation: One-hot encoding creates one column per category, so a feature with about 200,000 values produces a very wide, sparse matrix. That raises memory and training cost and can hurt tree models, which split poorly on many sparse indicators. Compact alternatives such as target encoding, feature hashing, or embeddings are usually preferred for high-cardinality features.

choiceRationales.A: Tree models can split on numeric indices, and many implementations handle categoricals natively, so one-hot encoding is not required.
choiceRationales.C: One-hot encoding adds one column per category and does not encode an order, so both claims are wrong.
choiceRationales.D: Indicator columns are 0/1 values and scaling does not fix the dimensionality problem.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 2.8: Identify and explain the model types or data sets for which one-hot encoding is or is not appropriate.

items.prompt: A data scientist is building models on a customer dataset that includes a nominal column, contract_type, with values month_to_month, one_year, and two_year. Which two model and data situations make one-hot encoding of this column appropriate? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Training a logistic regression model that cannot interpret category codes as meaningful numeric distances.
Training a Spark ML linear regression model, where integer indices would impose an artificial ordering and spacing on the categories.
Training a model on a column that has 50,000 distinct values and very little data per category.
Preparing a numeric column such as monthly_charges, so it can be treated as categorical.

items.explanation: Linear and logistic regression models treat numeric inputs as having magnitude and order. Integer-coding a nominal column would imply that one category is larger than another, so one-hot encoding is appropriate for them. One-hot encoding is a poor choice for very high-cardinality columns and is not meant for continuous numeric features.

choiceRationales.C: With 50,000 distinct values, one-hot encoding produces a huge sparse feature space, and sparse categories give weak signal. Other encodings are usually better.
choiceRationales.D: Continuous numeric features should generally be used as numbers, perhaps scaled or binned. One-hot encoding them would discard information and create many columns.

items.prompt: A data scientist is training a linear regression model to predict house sale price. The target column sale_price is strongly right-skewed, ranging from 50,000 to 20,000,000, and the model's residuals grow larger for higher-priced homes. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Apply a log transformation to sale_price before training, then convert predictions back with the exponential function
Apply a log transformation to sale_price only on the test set
One-hot encode sale_price so each price becomes its own category
Standardize sale_price with a StandardScaler and expect the skew to disappear

items.explanation: A log transformation compresses a long right tail and often stabilizes variance, which suits a linear regression whose residuals grow with the target. Predictions are then on the log scale, so they should be back-transformed with exp to report prices. The same transformation must be used in training and evaluation.

choiceRationales.B: Transforming only the test set makes the training and evaluation targets inconsistent and does not fix the training problem.
choiceRationales.C: One-hot encoding is for nominal categories. A continuous target would create thousands of useless columns.
choiceRationales.D: Standardizing shifts and rescales values but keeps the shape of the distribution, so the skew and heteroscedasticity remain.

choices.text: account_balance_usd, a strictly positive value that is right-skewed and spans several orders of magnitude
customer_age, which is roughly symmetric between 18 and 80
page_views, a right-skewed count of non-negative integers that includes many zeros (using log1p)
temperature_change, a roughly symmetric value that includes many negative numbers

items.explanation: Log transformations help right-skewed, non-negative features that span orders of magnitude. For counts that include zeros, log1p avoids taking the log of zero. Symmetric features and features with many negative values gain little and are not valid for a plain log.

choiceRationales.B: A roughly symmetric, narrow-range feature has no heavy tail to compress, so a log transform gives little benefit.
choiceRationales.D: The log is undefined for negative values and zero, and a symmetric feature does not need compression.

items.prompt: A data scientist has a labeled dataset of customer records and wants to group customers into segments for marketing, but no segment labels exist. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Logistic regression, using customer ID as the label
K-means clustering on scaled customer features
Linear regression on total spend
A random forest classifier trained on all features

items.explanation: Grouping records when no target labels exist is an unsupervised clustering problem. K-means is a standard clustering algorithm and works best when features are scaled, because it uses distances. The other options are supervised methods that need a meaningful target.

choiceRationales.A: Logistic regression is supervised and needs a meaningful class label. A customer ID is not a useful target.
choiceRationales.C: Linear regression predicts a continuous target. It does not discover segments.
choiceRationales.D: A random forest classifier is supervised and requires known class labels, which do not exist here.

Little preprocessing time is available. Which two algorithms are most appropriate? Choose two.

choices.text: Gradient-boosted trees classifier
K-means clustering
Linear regression
Random forest classifier

items.explanation: Churn yes/no is binary classification. Tree ensembles such as gradient-boosted trees and random forests handle nonlinear relationships and feature interactions, and need little feature scaling. K-means is unsupervised, and linear regression predicts continuous values and assumes a linear relationship.

choiceRationales.B: K-means is unsupervised clustering. It does not use the churn label and does not predict it.

items.prompt: A data scientist is training a Spark ML GBTClassifier to detect defective parts. Only 1% of the rows are defective. The data scientist wants the model to pay more attention to the minority class without changing the number of rows in the training data. Which approach should the data scientist use?

choices.text: Add a weight column that gives defective rows a higher weight and set it with weightCol on the estimator
Resample the test set so that it is balanced, then evaluate on that set
Drop the label column from the features so the model cannot learn the majority class
Increase the number of folds in CrossValidator so each fold has more minority rows

items.explanation: Class weights (or instance weights) make errors on minority rows count more in the loss. This changes the training objective without adding or removing rows. Estimators that support it take a weight column through a parameter such as weightCol. Note that GBTClassifier support for weightCol depends on the Spark version, so LogisticRegression or RandomForestClassifier are common examples.

choiceRationales.B: Resampling the test set distorts the evaluation and doesn't change how the model is trained. Evaluation data should reflect the real class distribution.
choiceRationales.C: The label is not a feature. Removing it from the features doesn't address imbalance, and the label is needed for supervised training.
choiceRationales.D: More folds don't change the class ratio. Cross-validation affects how performance is estimated, not how much weight the minority class gets in training.

items.prompt: A data scientist is building a classifier on a dataset where 3% of the examples are positive. The data scientist plans to rebalance the training data. Which two actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Split the data into train and test sets first, then oversample the minority class only in the training set
Oversample the minority class across the full dataset first, then split into train and test sets
Downsample the majority class in the training set, and evaluate on a test set that keeps the original class distribution
Rebalance the test set to 50/50 so that the reported metrics are more realistic

items.explanation: Rebalancing should be applied only to the training data, after the split. This keeps the test set representative of production data. Oversampling before splitting can put copies of the same minority rows in both train and test sets, which leaks information and inflates metrics. Rebalancing the test set makes metrics unrepresentative of real-world performance.

choiceRationales.B: Oversampling before the split duplicates minority rows into both train and test sets. This causes data leakage and overly optimistic metrics.
choiceRationales.D: A 50/50 test set doesn't match the real distribution, so metrics such as precision will not reflect production behavior.

items.prompt: A data scientist is building a Spark ML pipeline that includes a StandardScaler stage. The data scientist wants to know which object learns the column means and standard deviations from the training data, and which object then applies them to new data. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: StandardScaler is a transformer that learns the statistics in transform(), and StandardScalerModel is an estimator that applies them.
StandardScaler is an estimator that learns the statistics in fit(), and the resulting StandardScalerModel is a transformer that applies them in transform().
Both StandardScaler and StandardScalerModel are estimators, because scaling requires statistics from the data.
StandardScaler is an estimator that applies the statistics in transform(), and StandardScalerModel is a transformer that learns them in fit().

items.explanation: In Spark ML, an estimator implements fit() and returns a fitted model. StandardScaler learns the mean and standard deviation during fit(), and the resulting StandardScalerModel is a transformer. Its transform() method applies the learned statistics to any DataFrame.

choiceRationales.A: Reverses the roles. A transformer does not learn from data in transform(), and a fitted model is not an estimator.
choiceRationales.C: The fitted StandardScalerModel is a transformer, not an estimator. It has no fit() step.
choiceRationales.D: Learning happens in the estimator's fit(), not in the model's transform(). Applying the statistics is the model's job, so the roles are swapped.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.3: Compare estimators and transformers.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer is assembling a Spark ML pipeline for a churn model. Which two components are transformers rather than estimators when used in the pipeline? Choose two.

choices.text: A VectorAssembler that combines numeric columns into a single features vector column
A StringIndexer that maps category strings to indices based on label frequencies in the training data
A fitted LogisticRegressionModel returned by LogisticRegression.fit()
A RandomForestClassifier that has not yet been fit

items.explanation: A transformer implements transform() and needs no fitting. VectorAssembler is a pure transformer, and any fitted model such as LogisticRegressionModel is a transformer that adds prediction columns. StringIndexer and RandomForestClassifier are estimators because they must call fit() to learn from data.

choiceRationales.B: StringIndexer is an estimator. It must call fit() to learn the label-to-index mapping, and it returns a StringIndexerModel, which is the transformer.
choiceRationales.D: An unfitted RandomForestClassifier is an estimator. It becomes a transformer only as the RandomForestClassificationModel returned by fit().

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer trains a model with features from a Unity Catalog feature table and wants the logged model to carry the feature lookup information so that batch scoring and serving retrieve the same features automatically. Which approach should the engineer use?

choices.text: Join the feature table to the labels with a Spark join, train the model, and log it with mlflow.sklearn.log_model.
Create a training set with FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set using FeatureLookup objects, then log the model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model.
Export the feature table to a CSV file and reference its path in the model's MLflow tags.
Use the legacy FeatureStoreClient workspace feature store and register the model in a workspace model registry stage.

items.explanation: FeatureEngineeringClient.create_training_set takes FeatureLookup definitions and builds a training DataFrame. Logging the model with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model packages the feature lookup metadata with the model. At inference time, feature values can then be looked up automatically from the feature tables using only the lookup keys.

choiceRationales.A: A manual join trains fine, but the model is logged without feature metadata. Callers would have to recreate the join themselves at inference.
choiceRationales.C: Tags pointing to a CSV export do not give automatic feature lookup and create a stale copy of the data.
choiceRationales.D: The workspace feature store client and registry stages are legacy. The current practice is FeatureEngineeringClient with Unity Catalog.

items.prompt: A data scientist wants to use Hyperopt's `fmin` to find the hyperparameters that maximize validation accuracy of a classifier. Which objective function design is correct?

choices.text: Return the validation accuracy from the objective function, because `fmin` maximizes the returned value by default.
Return the negative of the validation accuracy (for example, `{'loss': -accuracy, 'status': STATUS_OK}`) from the objective function.
Return the validation accuracy and pass `mode='max'` to `fmin`.
Return the training accuracy so that `fmin` finds the model that fits the data best.

items.explanation: `fmin` always minimizes the value the objective function returns. To maximize a metric such as accuracy, return its negative as the loss. The search then drives the loss down, which raises accuracy.

choiceRationales.A: `fmin` minimizes the returned value. Returning raw accuracy would search for the lowest accuracy.
choiceRationales.C: `fmin` has no `mode` argument. Maximizing is done by negating the metric.
choiceRationales.D: Training accuracy rewards overfitting. The loss should come from validation data (or cross-validation) so the search favors models that generalize.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer defines a search space with `'kernel': hp.choice('kernel', ['linear', 'rbf'])` and runs `best = fmin(fn=objective, space=space, algo=tpe.suggest, max_evals=30)`. The result shows `{'kernel': 1}`, and the engineer wants to know which kernel that is. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: `fmin` returns the trained model that had the lowest loss, so `best` can be used directly for predictions.
For `hp.choice` parameters, `fmin` returns the index of the selected option rather than the option's value.
The value 1 is the lowest loss that was found during the 30 evaluations.
Calling `hyperopt.space_eval(space, best)` converts the result into the actual hyperparameter values, such as `'rbf'`.

items.explanation: `fmin` returns a dictionary of the best parameter settings. For `hp.choice`, it holds the index of the chosen option, so 1 means the second option, `'rbf'`. `space_eval(space, best)` maps those indices back to actual values.

choiceRationales.A: `fmin` returns a dictionary of best hyperparameters, not a fitted model. The model must be retrained with those values.
choiceRationales.C: The returned dictionary holds hyperparameter settings, not loss values. Losses are stored in the `Trials` object (or logged to MLflow).

items.prompt: A data scientist is using random search with scikit-learn's RandomizedSearchCV to tune a gradient boosting model. The learning rate could reasonably be anywhere from 0.00001 to 0.1. Which sampling distribution for the learning rate is most appropriate?

choices.text: A continuous uniform distribution from 0.00001 to 0.1
A discrete uniform distribution of integers from 1 to 100, divided by 1000
A log-uniform distribution from 0.00001 to 0.1
A normal distribution centered at 0.05

items.explanation: A hyperparameter that spans several orders of magnitude should be sampled on a log scale. A log-uniform distribution gives each order of magnitude (1e-5 to 1e-4, 1e-4 to 1e-3, and so on) about the same chance of being sampled. This lets random search explore the whole range efficiently.

choiceRationales.A: A linear uniform distribution puts about 90% of samples between 0.01 and 0.1. Small learning rates such as 1e-5 to 1e-3 would almost never be tried.
choiceRationales.B: This only produces values from 0.001 to 0.1 in steps of 0.001. It misses the lower orders of magnitude and again favors the larger values.
choiceRationales.D: A normal distribution centered at 0.05 concentrates samples near one value and can produce negative learning rates, which are invalid. It does not cover the small end of the range.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer runs a Spark ML CrossValidator with numFolds=5 over a large ParamGridBuilder grid, and the search takes too long. The cluster has idle capacity. Choose two changes that reduce the time of the search while still using a grid search.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer is tuning a Spark ML gradient-boosted tree model on a table with about 200 million labeled rows. The cluster budget is tight, and 20 hyperparameter combinations must be compared. Which validation strategy is the most reasonable?

choices.text: Use CrossValidator with numFolds=10, because more folds always produce a better final model.
Use CrossValidator, because a single validation split can never be representative of the data.
Use TrainValidationSplit, because a large validation set already gives a stable estimate and each combination is fit only once.
Skip validation and pick the combination with the best training metric, to avoid holding out any data.

items.explanation: With a very large dataset, a single validation split is already big enough to give a low-variance performance estimate. TrainValidationSplit fits each combination once, while k-fold cross-validation fits it k times. On a tight budget, the extra cost of cross-validation buys little.

choiceRationales.A: More folds do not always improve the final model. They mainly raise cost, and with this much data they add little reliability.
choiceRationales.B: A single split can be unrepresentative on small datasets. With 200 million rows, the validation set is large enough that this concern is minor.
choiceRationales.D: Training metrics reward overfitting, so selecting on them gives unreliable hyperparameter choices.

items.prompt: A data scientist has a labeled dataset of 2,000 rows and plans to compare 20 hyperparameter combinations using 5-fold cross-validation instead of a single train-validation split. Which two statements describe correct trade-offs of this choice? (Choose two.)

choices.text: The averaged validation metric depends less on which rows happened to land in one particular validation set.
Because each row is used for validation once, a separate held-out test set is no longer needed to estimate final performance.
Cross-validation guarantees that the selected model will not overfit the validation data.
Each combination must be fit five times, so the tuning cost is roughly five times that of a single split.

items.explanation: Averaging the metric across folds reduces sensitivity to one random split, which matters most on small datasets. The price is that every candidate is trained k times, so the search costs about k times more. Cross-validation does not remove the benefit of an untouched test set, and it does not guarantee against overfitting the selection process.

choiceRationales.B: The folds are used to select hyperparameters, so the resulting metric is optimistically biased. A separate test set is still the best way to estimate final performance.
choiceRationales.C: Selecting the best of many candidates by validation score can still overfit to the validation folds. Cross-validation reduces this risk but gives no guarantee.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer uses scikit-learn GridSearchCV with cv=5 on a training set and then logs the result with MLflow. Which two statements about the cross-validation behavior are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: The test set should be held out from GridSearchCV and used only once to estimate performance of the final selected model.
With the default refit=True, the best parameter combination is retrained on the full data passed to fit, and best_estimator_ is available.
For each parameter combination, the model is trained once on the full training data and scored on the same data five times.
The best_score_ attribute is the score of the refit model on the full training data.

items.explanation: GridSearchCV splits the data passed to fit into 5 folds, trains on 4 and scores on 1 for each combination, and averages the scores. With refit=True, it retrains the best combination on all of the data passed to fit. A separate held-out test set gives an unbiased final estimate because the CV data was used for selection.

choiceRationales.C: Each fold trains on a different subset and scores on the held-out fold, not on the same data.
choiceRationales.D: best_score_ is the mean cross-validated score of the best combination on held-out folds, not a score of the refit model on the full training data.

items.prompt: A data scientist runs scikit-learn's GridSearchCV with a parameter grid of n_estimators=[50, 100, 200] and max_depth=[5, 10], cv=5, and the default refit=True. How many models are fit in total, including the final refit?
items.explanation: The grid has 3 × 2 = 6 hyperparameter combinations. Each combination is fit once per fold, so the search fits 6 × 5 = 30 models. With refit=True, one more model is trained on the full training data using the best parameters, which gives 31.

choiceRationales.A: This counts only the parameter combinations and ignores that each one is fit once per cross-validation fold.
choiceRationales.B: This is the number of fits during the search (6 × 5). It leaves out the final refit on the full data that refit=True performs.
choiceRationales.D: This wrongly multiplies the 6 combinations by 5 folds plus one refit per combination, (6 + 1) × 5. The refit happens once, only for the best parameters.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.10: Identify the number of models being trained in conjunction with a grid-search and cross-validation process. A blind second pass chose D (35); C (31) was confirmed by hand: 6 x 5 = 30 fits plus one refit.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer builds a Spark ML ParamGrid with 3 values for regParam, 2 values for elasticNetParam, and 2 values for maxIter, which gives 12 combinations. The engineer is comparing CrossValidator with numFolds=3 against TrainValidationSplit on this grid. Which two statements about the number of models fit during the search, before any final refit, are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: CrossValidator fits 12 models, because the fold models share the same parameters and are reused.
CrossValidator fits 36 models.
TrainValidationSplit fits 36 models, because it evaluates each combination on three splits.
TrainValidationSplit fits 12 models.

items.explanation: CrossValidator fits one model per combination per fold, so 12 × 3 = 36. TrainValidationSplit uses a single train/validation split, so it fits one model per combination, which is 12. Both then refit the best parameters on the full dataset, which is not counted here.

choiceRationales.A: Models are not reused across folds. Each fold trains on different data, so each combination is fit once per fold.
choiceRationales.C: TrainValidationSplit evaluates on one split only, so it fits one model per combination. The count of 36 applies to 3-fold CrossValidator.

items.prompt: A data scientist is building a binary classifier to flag defective parts. The downstream system uses the predicted probabilities directly to estimate expected repair cost, so the probabilities must be well calibrated. Which metric is most appropriate for comparing candidate models on this need?

choices.text: Accuracy at a threshold of 0.5
Log loss
Recall at a threshold of 0.5
F1 score at a threshold of 0.5

items.explanation: Log loss (cross-entropy) is computed from the predicted probabilities and penalizes confident wrong predictions heavily. It therefore rewards well-calibrated probabilities. Accuracy, recall, and F1 use hard labels after a threshold and ignore how close the probabilities are to the true outcomes.

choiceRationales.A: Accuracy uses thresholded labels, so probabilities of 0.51 and 0.99 count the same. It says nothing about calibration.
choiceRationales.C: Recall only measures the share of true positives found at one threshold. It ignores false positives and probability quality.
choiceRationales.D: F1 combines precision and recall at a single threshold. It is a label-based metric and does not assess probability quality.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.11: Use common classification metrics: F1, Log Loss, ROC/AUC, etc.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer evaluates a binary classifier on a held-out set and plots the ROC curve. Which two statements about the ROC curve and AUC are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: The ROC curve plots precision against recall across decision thresholds.
An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to a model that ranks positives and negatives no better than random.
The ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across decision thresholds.
AUC changes if the decision threshold is moved from 0.5 to 0.3.

items.explanation: The ROC curve plots true positive rate (y-axis) against false positive rate (x-axis) as the threshold varies. AUC summarizes ranking quality across all thresholds, and 0.5 means no better than random ranking. Because it aggregates over every threshold, it does not change when you pick a particular one.

choiceRationales.A: Precision versus recall is the precision-recall curve, not the ROC curve.
choiceRationales.D: AUC is computed across all thresholds, so choosing a particular operating threshold does not change it.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.11: Use common classification metrics: F1, Log Loss, ROC/AUC, etc.

items.prompt: A data scientist trains a regression model to predict delivery time in minutes and evaluates it on a held-out validation set. Which two statements about regression metrics are correct? (Choose two.)

choices.text: MAE is always greater than or equal to RMSE for the same predictions.
RMSE is expressed in the same units as the target, so an RMSE of 6 means a typical error on the order of 6 minutes, with larger errors weighted more.
An R-squared of 0.85 means that 85% of the individual predictions are within 15% of the actual values.
R-squared can be negative on validation data if the model fits worse than a baseline that always predicts the mean of the target.

items.explanation: RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error, so it is in the target's units and penalizes large errors more than small ones. R-squared compares the model's squared error with that of a mean-only baseline. On new data, a model that does worse than that baseline gets a negative value.

choiceRationales.A: Reversed. Squaring before averaging gives large errors more weight, so RMSE is always greater than or equal to MAE.
choiceRationales.C: R-squared is the proportion of target variance explained by the model. It says nothing about the share of predictions within a percentage tolerance.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.12: Use common regression metrics: RMSE, MAE, R-squared, etc.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer builds a Spark ML CrossValidator with a RegressionEvaluator and compares two configurations: one with metricName="rmse" and one with metricName="r2". How does CrossValidator choose the best model in each case?

choices.text: It always picks the model with the highest average metric value, so the rmse configuration must be changed to a negative RMSE first.
It always picks the model with the lowest average metric value, for both rmse and r2.
It uses the evaluator's isLargerBetter setting, so it picks the lowest average RMSE and the highest average R-squared.
It ranks models by the metric on the training folds, and only uses the validation fold to compute the final report.

items.explanation: Spark's evaluators report whether a larger value of the metric is better. For RegressionEvaluator, rmse, mse, and mae are minimized, while r2 and var are maximized. CrossValidator averages the metric across the validation folds and selects the best parameter set accordingly, so no manual sign flipping is needed.

choiceRationales.A: This is the scikit-learn scoring convention, where error metrics are negated. Spark ML handles direction through isLargerBetter instead.
choiceRationales.B: Minimizing R-squared would select the worst-fitting model. The direction depends on the metric.
choiceRationales.D: CrossValidator scores each candidate on the held-out validation fold of each split, not on the training folds.

items.prompt: A data scientist is building a model to flag defective parts on a manufacturing line. Only 1% of parts are defective, and missing a defective part is far more costly than inspecting a good part by mistake. Which metric should the data scientist prioritize when comparing models?

choices.text: Accuracy
Recall for the defective class
R-squared
Precision for the non-defective class

items.explanation: When false negatives are the costly error, recall on the positive (defective) class measures how many true defects the model catches. Accuracy is misleading with 1% positives, because predicting all parts as good scores 99%. R-squared is a regression metric.

choiceRationales.A: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class here. A model that never flags a defect would score about 99%.
choiceRationales.C: R-squared is a regression metric and does not apply to a classification task.
choiceRationales.D: Precision on the non-defective class is dominated by the majority class and does not measure how many defects are caught.

draft.notes: Exam guide objective 3.13: Choose the most appropriate metric for a given scenario objective.

items.prompt: A machine learning engineer is training a regression model to forecast daily demand for products whose volumes range from a few units to many thousands. The business wants an error measure that is expressed in the same units as demand and is not dominated by a few large outliers. Which two metrics are most appropriate? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Mean absolute error (MAE)
Mean squared error (MSE)
Median absolute error
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)

items.explanation: MAE and median absolute error are both in the same units as the target. They do not square the errors, so large outliers have much less influence than with squared-error metrics. MSE squares errors and is in squared units. AUC is a classification metric.

choiceRationales.B: MSE squares the errors, so it is in squared units and is dominated by large errors and outliers.
choiceRationales.D: AUC evaluates classifiers and does not apply to a continuous regression target.
